subject: Start sampling from well equilibrated values from previous run

messages.author: 11cd7b0c99a3bee8
messages.subject: Start sampling from well equilibrated values from previous run
parts:
Good morning,
 
I am starting chains from well equilibrated initial values, which I obtain from a previous run. It seems that during warmup, stan nonetheless starts to explore solutions quite far away from initial values. Are there optuions with which I can tell stan to start sampling smoothly since the initial values are of high quality?
 
 
Context: I have a large data set (15000 subjects with 20 measurements per subject). Running the model on all the data would take weeks. Thus I make long runs on 200 subjects to make sure that the chains converge and that good initial values are generated. The good initial values are then used to start short parallel runs with limited equilibration using all data.
 
Best regards,
 
Christian Bartels
Novartis Pharma AG
Basel

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Start sampling from well equilibrated values from previous run
parts:
Per usual I have to advocate caution in these matters. The problem is that as you add more data the neighborhood
of high posterior mass shrinks, so "equilibrated" values for small data may in fact be far away from equilibrium when
you add more data.

That said, my guess here is that adaptation is amplifying any changes as it tries to relearn the local curvature.

One option is to turn adaptation off entirely (sample adapt engaged=0) and set the step size to a previously learned value
(sample algorithm=hmc stepsize=0.001). We do not yet have the capability of setting the metric explicitly. The issue here
is that the optimal step size will likely shrink with more data so you'd want to allow adaptation.

Another option is to allow the step size to adapt but not the metric (sample algorithm=hmc metric=unit_e). If your
parameters have varying scales this will lead to much less efficient sampling but smoother adaptation.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Start sampling from well equilibrated values from previous run
parts:
I'm not sure exactly what you mean by starting smoothly.

Unless you explicitly turn adaptation off, Stan's going
to start from your initial values and adapt both a diagonal mass
matrix (roughly inverse scales of the various parameters) and
a step size. Step size gets adapted based on a target acceptance
probability and the mass matrix is estimated from warmup samples
in increasingly large blocks (always using only the last half or
so of the warmup iterations for the next estimate in order to
forget bad starting points).

The next release of Stan (2.1.0) will make the warmup more
flexible in terms of windows, but it's not clear that if you dramatically
up the data size that the same step sizes and mass matrix will be applicable.
I'm sure Michael has a better handle on this than I do.

- Bob

messages.author: 11cd7b0c99a3bee8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Start sampling from well equilibrated values from previous run
parts:
Dear Bob and Michael,
 
Thanks for your suggestions and comments. I'm after efficient sampling, in general, and in getting the sampling started without the need of many warmup iterations. This is what I meant when I referred to "starting smoothly" . Currently there is a bump in the trace plots at about iteration 10 when I fit 200 subjects. And when fitting all the 17112 subjects, stan makes the first 9 iterations within ~1 minute, and then "stalls" (= it takes more than 1h) at iteration 10.
 
I tried out your suggestions. This seems not to improve the situation. One thing I will do, is to wait longer, and see whether stan finishes within the next days.
 
If anyone has ideas, I have copied in below the core of the model, the dimensions, and the code I use to start the run.

K=12, nid=17112, ndat=327203, nDT=5 (this implies 205344 individual parameters)
 
sflist1<-mclapply(1:8,mc.cores=8,
  function(i) stan(fit=modelComp
  ,data=data
  ,iter=200
  ,warmup=100
  ,thin=1
  ,chains=1                  
    ,chain_id=i
    ,pars=pars
    ,init=initsRunin
    ,refresh=1
    ,verbose=TRUE
    #,control=list(stepsize_jitter=1.0)
    ,diagnostic_file=paste("diagnostic_",i,".csv",sep="")
    ,sample_file=paste("sample_",i,".csv",sep="")
    ,seed=i))
parameters {
// population mean values
    vector[K] mu;
// between subject variability
    vector<lower=0>[K] sigma;
// correlations
    corr_matrix[K] Omega;
// individual parameters
    vector[K] eta[nid];
// residual errors
    real<lower=0> res[nDT];        // residual errors
}
transformed parameters {
 cov_matrix[K] Sigma;     // covariance matrix
 vector[nObsMT[1]] IPRE1; // normally distributed predictions
 vector[nObsMT[1]] RES1; // normally distributed predictions
 vector[nObsMT[2]+nObsMT[3]] LAMBDA2;  // poisson rate
 
 // calculate covariance matrix
 for (m in 1:K) Sigma[m,m] <- sigma[m] * sigma[m] * Omega[m,m];
 for (m in 1:(K-1)) {
  for (n in (m+1):K) {
   Sigma[m,n] <- sigma[m] * sigma[n] * Omega[m,n];
   Sigma[n,m] <- Sigma[m,n];
  }
 }
...
}
model {
// data
    DV1 ~ normal(IPRE1,RES1);
    CNT2 ~ poisson(exp(LAMBDA2));
// hierarchical model
 for(i in 1:nid) eta[i] ~ multi_normal(mu,Sigma); 
// vague priors on parameters
 mu ~ normal(0,10);
 Omega ~ lkj_corr(2.0);
 sigma ~ normal(0,10); // cauchy(0,5);
 res ~ normal(0,10); // cauchy(0,5);
// problem specific priors
...
}

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Start sampling from well equilibrated values from previous run
parts:
Christian,

Just to verify, you run the below code first then run again with adaptation off?

If adaptation is off and you're seeing huge variations in iteration timing then you're likely dealing with a very nasty posterior (a consequence of concentration of measure with increasing dimension that I had mentioned before). This is very common in hierarchical models where there are tails with very high curvature that cause HMC to become numerically unstable and get stuck (same thing happens with other sampling algorithms and it's all a consequence of the geometry of the underlying distribution).

That said, there is a lot you can improve in your model. Firstly, use poisson_log() intend of poisson(exp( ) ). Secondly, you need to use a non-centered parameterization for the eta[i], a la

hat_eta[i] ~ multi_normal(0, 1) // Actually faster to define hat_eta as a matrix and use vectorization with the univariate normal(0, 1) here
eta[i] <- Sigma * hat_eta[i] + mu

This will go a long way to improving the geometry of your posterior and dramatically speed up sampling (in big hierarchical models it's not uncommon to get speed ups of a few orders of magnitude).
